title: Fine-grained analytics RBAC: service-layer permissions and query filters for usage views
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Background: The console exposes multiple analytics endpoints (e.g., /usage/views, /analytics/query, /dashboards/export) that surface customer usage and cost breakdowns. Currently, much of the access control is enforced client-side (UI) or via coarse org-level checks in the gateway. This creates gaps where API tokens, direct API calls, or pipeline consumers can access or export data beyond intended RBAC scopes.

Problem statement: Implement service-layer RBAC for analytics endpoints and ensure data pipelines enforce row-level and dataset-level permissions so that: (1) only authorized roles can view or export sensitive usage views; (2) tenant isolation is preserved across Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployments; and (3) audit trails capture who queried what and when.

Goals and acceptance criteria: 
- Backend authorization enforces role/permission checks for all analytics endpoints and returns 403s for unauthorized query attempts.
- Query-level filters (org_id/team_id/dataset_id) are applied in the analytics API and pipelines to prevent cross-tenant leakage.
- Export endpoints (CSV/JSON) require explicit export permission and emit an audit event with user, scope, and query hash.
- Audit logs are searchable in Console and stored for the configured retention period.
- Migration path exists: existing tokens and integrations are evaluated, and a compatibility mode is available during rollout.

Proposed implementation approach: 
1) AuthZ model: extend the existing AuthN/AuthZ service with a new resource type analytics_view and actions [read, query, export, manage]. Map roles (org_admin, billing_admin, analyst, viewer) to permission sets. Store permissions in the existing RBAC store (Postgres + cache).
2) Service-layer enforcement: add middleware to console-backend and analytics-api that performs permission checks before executing queries. Use a compact permission check API: /authz/check?subject={user_or_token}&resource=analytics_view:{view_id}&action=query.
3) Query filtering: require that all analytics queries include a canonical context (org_id, team_id, dataset_id). For direct SQL paths used by pipeline jobs, add a query-rewrite layer that injects WHERE org_id = :org_id AND dataset_id IN (:allowed_datasets). For Pre-aggregations, annotate rows with _org_id and enforce row-level security in the analytics warehouse (BigQuery/ClickHouse).
4) Token and integration migration: detect tokens lacking scoped permissions and tag them as legacy_insecure. Provide a one-click migration in console to scope tokens by org and dataset. During canary, legacy tokens continue to work for 48 hours before enforced.
5) Audit logging: emit structured audit events to the analytics event stream with fields [actor_id, actor_type, resource, action, query_hash, timestamp, permissions_check]. Surface a view in Console where security teams can filter by actor/resource/time.
6) Tests and safeguards: unit tests for AuthZ checks, integration tests simulating cross-tenant queries, and a chaos test to ensure fallback behavior for pipeline consumers.
7) Metrics and monitoring: dashboard tracking 403 rates, permission-check latency, denied query counts, and export events. Create alerts for spikes in denied accesses or permission-check errors.

Data pipeline considerations: 
- Ingestion: pipeline jobs must stamp events with org_id and dataset_id on ingress. If missing, reject the event and emit a dlq entry with reason=org_missing.
- Materialized views and rollups: ensure rollups carry _org_id and are partitioned by org_id to make RLS efficient.
- Downstream consumers (billing, ML-evals): require a service-account-based permission model; grant least-privilege dataset access and rotate credentials on rollout.

Rollout and migration plan: 
- Phase 0 (week 0): merge AuthZ schema changes behind a feature flag; add permission enums and small middleware that logs intended checks but does not enforce.
- Phase 1 (week 1-2): opt-in canary for 5 internal orgs and QA; enable enforcement for read/query actions only; provide migration dashboard for tokens.
- Phase 2 (week 3): enable export restriction and audit logging for all orgs; start filtering pipeline ingestions for org_id.
- Phase 3 (week 4): enforcement for all actions; deprecate legacy token compatibility after 48-hour warnings and email notifications.

Risks and mitigations: 
- Performance impact: permission checks may add latency. Mitigation: cache AuthZ decisions for short TTLs and batch checks for multi-resource queries.
- Migration friction: customers with many integrations may break. Mitigation: compatibility mode, tooling to bulk-scope tokens, and clear communication with support playbook.
- Data pipeline complexity: adding org_id stamping requires changes across ingestion producers. Mitigation: provide client libraries and a shim service to backfill metadata for legacy producers.

Dependencies: GH PRs for console-backend and analytics-api, design doc, and security review.

Links and artifacts: 
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ANALYTICS/RBAC+Design
- Implementation PR (console): https://github.com/redwood/console/pull/4321
- Pipeline changes PR: https://github.com/redwood/analytics-pipelines/pull/2105
- Risk/incident notes: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/analytics-rbac-incident-learnings
